newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Noon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Noon Update.

text.p: SCOTT MILLER'S SCHOLARSHIP LOSS TO BE PROBED
Australian Swimming officials have launched an investigation into an incident which resulted in Scott Miller's scholarship at the Australian Institute of Sport being terminated.
The AIS says Miller failed to train properly during the
Australian swim team's butterfly and backstroke camp last week and there was no option but to end his scholarship.
The decision has put the Olympic silver medalist's spot in the Australian team for the Pan Pacific meet in doubt.
DAIRY INDUSTRY TOLD TO THINK TWICE ABOUT DEREGULATING
Australia's dairy industry has been warned to be cautious before accepting deregulation.
The calls come as dairy farmers across the Hunter region in New South Wales meet in Singleton to discuss the national competition policy, otherwise known as the Hilmer Report.
Jim Begg, of the United Kingdom's Dairy Industry Federation, says the move to deregulation has been difficult for UK dairy processers and it initially led to a drop in the price of milk.
Mr Begg says while the market is now stronger in the UK, it is important local producers do not take the discussions lightly.
BEAZLEY SAYS VAT WOULD NOT CLAMP DOWN ON CASH ECONOMY
Opposition leader, Kim Beazley, says tax avoidance is best fought by measures other than the introduction of a value added tax, or VAT.
Treasurer, Peter Costello, says a V-A-T could help prevent billions of dollars being lost to the black economy, where cash transactions can be hidden from the tax office.
But the Opposition says the introduction of a V-A-T in other countries has not had that effect.
Mr Beazley says stricter enforcement is the only way to tame the black economy.
The Society of Certified Practising Accountants is also at odds with the Treasurer.
The society's Richard Vann says such a tax would make only a small impact on the cash economy.
Professor Vann says people in the cash economy would pay taxes on stock under a VAT or GST but would recover it by putting up prices.
CORRUPTION WATCHDOG TARGETS WA POLICE
The MP who sparked the Woods Royal Commission into the New South Wales Police force believes a similar inquiry is needed in Western Australia.
Former Indepedent MP, John Hatton, dropped a bombshell in the New South Wales Parliament when he accused several senior officers of being corrupt.
He says police are skilled in the distortion, destruction and presentation of evidence and a completely independent body is needed to investigate police corruption.
Mr Hatton says pressure needs to be maintained on the West
Australian Government to hold a Royal Commission.
AUSTRALIA TO OPPOSE MOVES TO RE-OPEN TRADE IN IVORY
The Federal Government has decided to oppose moves by African nations to lift a global ban on trade in ivory.
Zimbabwe, Namibia and Botswana have applied to end trade
restrictions on the African elephant, to be discussed at an international environment conference in Harare next week.
Federal Environment Minister, Robert Hill, says Australia will lobby other countries to oppose the move, and an attempt by South Africa to downlist the Southern White Rhinoceros.
Senator Hill says lifting the ban on ivory would only encourage poaching, and the renewed destruction of elephants.
BOY, 15, REMANDED IN CUSTODY ON MURDER CHARGE
A 15-year-old boy charged with murdering a man from Metford, near Newcastle in New South Wales, last week has been remanded in custody for another month.
A Children's Court Magistrate in Newcastle this morning refused a bail application from the boy's solicitor, the case against him is a strong one.
The 15-year-old is charged with murdering 47-year-old Phillip White last Wednesday night.
The man's body was found by family members near the Metford railway Station the following morning.
He had suffered severe head and facial injuries.
In Maitland Children's Court last week, police alledged the boy admitted hitting Mr White about the head with a large rock after an argument at the station.
The Worimi Children's Court Magistrate this morning refused bail, on the grounds of a strong prosecution case, and a strong chance the accused would commit further offences if released from custody.
The case will come back before the court in early July.
WINE EXPORTS ON THE RISE
Wines exports for the financial year are up by 24 per cent over the year before.
Authorities say nearly 156 million litres have been exported, valued at nearly $595 million to the end of May.
That's a 31 per cent rise in value.
SA NEARING END OF FIRE BLIGHT SURVEY
The search for fire blight in South Australia's commercial apple and pear orchards is nearly finished.
The Primary Industries Department says nearly 2,300 hectares of the state's orchards have been surveyed, with only 100 hectares to go.
The last trees are being checked today in the Barossa Valley and the south-east.
Preliminary results from Germany on plant samples sent from the Adelaide Botanic Gardens have failed to confirm the presence of the plant disease, which can devastate trees, but does not harm fruit.
Authorities say further tests may take up to four weeks for a conclusive result.
